title: How Foot Binding Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain footbinding, the Chinese custom of binding girls' feet to make them small and pointed, which lasted roughly a thousand years (c. 970 to the 1950s) and affected about three billion women. The episode covers its supposed origin at the court of Emperor Li Yu and his ballerina favorite, the binding process (soaking in hot water and animal blood, breaking toes, bandaging, the three-inch "lotus" foot), the risks of gangrene and infection, its status role and how it limited women's mobility, its effects on Chinese architecture and on China's lack of exploration, the erotic and fetish culture around bound feet, wedding shoes with erotic embroidery, and its end under missionaries, social Darwinist reformers, natural foot societies, government inspectors, and finally Communist labor policies. Ends with a listener mail segment about Brown Water Coffee and a Netflix ad.

segments.title: Opening banter and congratulations
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, congratulating Kristen Bell on her baby and mentioning the Veronica Mars movie, then introduce the topic of foot binding.

segments.title: Origins of footbinding at Li Yu's court
segments.summary: Overview of footbinding as a practice lasting about a thousand years in China, affecting roughly three billion women. The origin story involves Emperor Li Yu, his ballerina favorite who danced on a golden lotus pedestal with bound feet, and other court women copying her. It began as a status symbol among wealthy women.

segments.title: What bound feet looked like
segments.summary: Describes the resulting foot, about three inches long and pointed, with the heel separated and the arch permanently formed, and how the practice spread across China and limited manual labor.

segments.title: End of footbinding: missionaries, reformers and natural foot societies
segments.summary: Discusses the decline of footbinding, citing Western missionaries, social Darwinists worried about national strength, an education campaign with three phases, natural foot societies whose members pledged not to bind or marry bound-footed partners, and government inspectors enforcing a ban.

segments.title: The binding process and its dangers
segments.summary: Step-by-step description of binding a young girl's feet: soaking in hot water and animal blood, removing dead skin, clipping toenails, applying talc, wrapping in long cotton bandages soaked to shrink, folding toes under and breaking foot bones, then walking in small shoes. Risks include infection, gangrene, and loss of shape if unwrapped.

segments.title: Social, architectural and historical effects
segments.summary: Covers the effects of footbinding on women's mobility, male dominance, architecture built for women to lean on walls, and China's reduced exploration and colonization, contrasted with non-binding regions that colonized other places. Notes that many surviving women expressed pride in their bound feet.

segments.title: Erotic culture, fetish and bound-foot shoes
segments.summary: Discusses the erotic fetish around bound feet, including odd practices with the bathwater and shoes, pustules and smell, an erotic sex manual, many pairs of shoes per woman, and wedding shoes with erotic embroidery used by newlyweds.

segments.title: Closing and Communist end note
segments.summary: Hosts note that Communists ended footbinding through labor demands and that it is now said to have died out, then close the episode.
